q: Rank the C–H bonds on the tagged carbons a, b and c from weakest to strongest (homolytic bond dissociation energy).
h: More s character in the carbon orbital makes a shorter, stronger C–H bond. Also ask whether the radical left behind could be resonance-stabilized.
w: C–H bond strength rises with s character: sp3 (25% s) < sp2 (33%) < sp (50%). The alkyne C–H on a is the strongest (about 556 kJ/mol), the vinyl C–H on b is next (about 465 kJ/mol), and the CH3 C–H on c is weakest. Carbon c is also allylic, so breaking its C–H gives a resonance-stabilized radical, which lowers its BDE even further (about 370 kJ/mol). Order: c < b < a.
x: This reverses the trend; higher s character holds the bonding electrons closer to carbon and makes the C–H bond stronger, so the sp C–H is the strongest.
The allylic CH<sub>3</sub> C–H is weaker than a vinyl C–H: it is sp<sup>3</sup> and its radical is resonance-stabilized, while a vinyl radical is not.
The alkyne C–H (sp, 50% s) is the strongest of the three, not weaker than the vinyl C–H.

q:
Rank the molecular dipole moments from smallest to largest.
I. CH2Cl2   II. CHCl3   III. CCl4
h: More polar bonds do not always mean a larger molecular dipole. Think about how the C–Cl vectors cancel in a tetrahedron.
w: CCl4 is perfectly tetrahedral, so its four C–Cl dipoles cancel (μ = 0). In CHCl3 three C–Cl dipoles partly cancel one another, leaving about 1.0 D. In CH2Cl2 only two C–Cl dipoles at about 112° add, and they reinforce more than they cancel, giving about 1.6 D. Order: III < II < I.
x: Adding chlorines adds polar bonds, but in a tetrahedron the extra C–Cl dipoles point in opposing directions and cancel; CCl<sub>4</sub> has μ = 0.
CCl<sub>4</sub> is the smallest (zero), but CHCl<sub>3</sub> (about 1.0 D) is smaller than CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (about 1.6 D), because a third C–Cl bond partly cancels the other two.
CCl<sub>4</sub> has zero dipole by symmetry, so it must be the smallest, not in the middle.

q: Rank these C5H12 isomers from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Only London dispersion forces act here. Which shape gives the most surface contact between neighboring molecules?
w: All three isomers have the same mass, so the difference comes from shape. Branching makes a molecule more compact (closer to a sphere), which lowers the contact area and the London dispersion forces. Neopentane (III, 9.5 °C) < isopentane (II, 28 °C) < pentane (I, 36 °C): III < II < I.
x: This is reversed: the linear isomer has the most surface contact and the strongest dispersion forces, so it boils highest.
Isopentane is less branched than neopentane, so it boils higher than III, not lower.
Pentane, with the most surface area, has the highest boiling point, not the middle one.

q: These compounds have similar molar masses (72–74 g/mol). Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each pure liquid: dispersion only, dipole–dipole, or hydrogen bonding.
w: Diethyl ether (I) has a small dipole and no O–H, so it relies mostly on dispersion (bp 35 °C). Butanal (II) has a strongly polar C=O and dipole–dipole attractions (bp 75 °C). Butan-1-ol (III) can hydrogen-bond to itself through O–H (bp 117 °C). Order: I < II < III.
x: The C=O group of an aldehyde is much more polar than the C–O–C of an ether, so the aldehyde boils higher than the ether.
Butan-1-ol hydrogen-bonds to itself; the aldehyde cannot (it has no O–H), so the alcohol boils highest.
This is the reverse; the alcohol, with H bonding, has the highest boiling point.

q: Which compound is miscible with water in all proportions?
h: Both ethers accept hydrogen bonds from water. Which oxygen is easier for a water molecule to reach?
w: Water dissolves an ether by donating H bonds to the oxygen lone pairs. In tetrahydrofuran the ring ties the alkyl groups back, leaving the oxygen lone pairs exposed, so THF is completely miscible with water. In diethyl ether the freely rotating ethyl groups crowd the oxygen, and the compound dissolves only to about 7 g per 100 mL. Pentane and 1-chlorobutane cannot accept H bonds well and are nearly insoluble.
x: Diethyl ether has the same number of carbons and an O atom, but its ethyl groups shield the oxygen; it is only partly soluble (about 7 g/100 mL).
Pentane has only C–C and C–H bonds; it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor and is insoluble in water.
The C–Cl bond is polar, but chlorine is a very weak H-bond acceptor, so 1-chlorobutane is nearly insoluble in water.

q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself in the pure liquid?
h: A hydrogen bond needs both a donor (H on N, O or F) and an acceptor (a lone pair on N, O or F).
w: N-Methylacetamide has an N–H donor and a C=O acceptor, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other (as in protein backbones). Trimethylamine, acetone and ethyl acetate have lone-pair acceptors but no H on N or O, so they can accept H bonds from water but cannot H-bond to themselves.
x: All three N substituents are methyl groups; with no N–H, trimethylamine has no donor.
Acetone's oxygen is an acceptor, but its hydrogens are on carbon and C–H is not an H-bond donor.
The ester has two oxygen acceptors but no O–H or N–H donor.

q: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene boils at 60 °C, while the trans isomer boils at 48 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: The cis isomer has a net dipole and dipole–dipole attractions; the trans isomer’s bond dipoles cancel
The cis isomer can hydrogen-bond through its C–H bonds, while the trans isomer cannot do so
The cis isomer has a larger molar mass and therefore stronger London dispersion forces between molecules
The trans isomer is more strained, which weakens its attractions to neighboring molecules
h: The isomers have the same mass and formula. What property differs because of how the C–Cl bonds are arranged?
w: Both isomers have the same atoms and nearly the same surface area. In the trans isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel (μ = 0), while in the cis isomer they add to a net dipole (about 1.9 D). The cis molecules attract each other through dipole–dipole forces in addition to dispersion, so the cis isomer boils higher.
x: C–H bonds are not hydrogen-bond donors; neither isomer can H-bond to itself.
Stereoisomers have identical formulas and molar masses, so mass cannot explain the difference.
Ring or steric strain is an intramolecular energy term and does not set boiling point; trans-alkenes are actually the less strained isomers.

q: Acetic acid (60 g/mol) boils at 118 °C, while propan-1-ol (60 g/mol) boils at 97 °C. What is the best explanation?
c: Acetic acid forms cyclic dimers held by two strong hydrogen bonds
Acetic acid has more hydrogen-bond donors per molecule than propan-1-ol
Propan-1-ol is nonpolar because its O–H dipole is canceled by the alkyl chain
Acetic acid is ionized in the pure liquid, so ion–ion forces raise its boiling point
h: Count donors and acceptors in a carboxylic acid, and picture two molecules facing each other.
w: Both compounds have one O–H donor. A carboxylic acid also has a C=O oxygen that is a strong acceptor, so two molecules can line up head-to-head and form a cyclic dimer held by two hydrogen bonds. The resonance in the COOH group makes its O–H more polarized and its C=O oxygen more electron-rich, so these H bonds are stronger than an alcohol's. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so acetic acid boils higher.
x: Each molecule has exactly one O–H donor, so the difference is not the number of donors but the strength and pairing of the H bonds.
Propan-1-ol is polar and hydrogen-bonds to itself; that is why it boils far above propane or butane of similar mass.
Pure acetic acid is a weak acid and is almost entirely un-ionized; the liquid is held together by hydrogen bonds, not ions.

q: Which statement about the π and π* molecular orbitals of ethene is correct?
c: π* has a nodal plane between the two carbons, perpendicular to the C=C axis, and is the LUMO
π has a nodal plane between the two carbons, and that is why it is lower in energy than π*
π* holds the two π electrons in the ground state and is the HOMO
The π electron density is concentrated along the C–C internuclear axis
h: Combine two parallel p orbitals in phase and out of phase. Which combination puts a node between the nuclei?
w: Adding the two p orbitals in phase gives the bonding π MO, with electron density above and below the C–C axis and no node between the carbons; it holds both π electrons and is the HOMO. The out-of-phase combination is π*, which has a nodal plane between the carbons perpendicular to the bond axis. It is empty, higher in energy, and is the LUMO. (Both MOs also share the nodal plane of the molecule itself.)
x: The bonding π MO has no node between the carbons; a node between nuclei raises the energy, which is why π* is higher.
The two π electrons fill the lower-energy bonding π MO, which is the HOMO; π* is empty in the ground state.
Density along the internuclear axis describes a σ bond; π density lies above and below the plane of the molecule.

q: Why does cis-but-2-ene not convert to trans-but-2-ene at room temperature?
c: Rotating about the C=C bond would twist the p orbitals apart and break the π bond
The two methyl groups are too large to pass each other during rotation
Both carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>, and their σ bond cannot rotate
The cis isomer is more stable than the trans isomer, so there is no driving force
h: What holds the two halves of a double bond in one orientation that a single bond does not have?
w: The π bond exists only while the two p orbitals are parallel. Rotating one carbon 90° makes the p orbitals perpendicular, so the overlap drops to zero and the π bond breaks, which costs roughly 250–270 kJ/mol. That is far more energy than is available at room temperature, so cis and trans alkenes are separate, isolable compounds.
x: Methyl groups pass each other easily in butane (single-bond rotation barrier only about 25 kJ/mol); the problem is the π bond, not size.
The alkene carbons are sp<sup>2</sup>; σ bonds alone rotate freely, so a pure σ bond would not prevent isomerization.
The trans isomer is actually the more stable one, so there is a driving force; the barrier, not thermodynamics, prevents the change.

q: The C=C bond of ethene is stronger than the C–C bond of ethane, but less than twice as strong. Why?
c: The π bond is formed by side-on p-orbital overlap, which is weaker than the head-on overlap of a σ bond
The π bond is formed by head-on overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals, which is weaker than p-orbital overlap
The two carbons of ethene are farther apart than those of ethane, so both bonds are weakened
The π electrons are shared with the hydrogens, so less of their density is between the carbons
h: Compare how much overlap two orbitals get when they meet end-to-end versus side-by-side.
w: A double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond. The σ component forms by head-on overlap of sp2 orbitals, which concentrates density between the nuclei. The π component forms by side-on overlap of parallel p orbitals, which is less effective, so the π bond is weaker than a σ bond. The total is therefore less than twice a C–C single bond. This weak π bond is the reactive site of alkenes.
x: Head-on overlap of hybrid orbitals makes the σ bond; the π bond uses unhybridized p orbitals overlapping side by side.
The C=C bond (about 1.34 Å) is shorter than the C–C bond in ethane (1.54 Å), not longer.
The π MO is made only from the two carbon p orbitals; the hydrogens bond through σ bonds and are not part of the π system.

q: What is the LUMO of the tert-butyl cation, the orbital that accepts electrons from an incoming nucleophile?
c: The empty 2p orbital on the central carbon
An sp<sup>3</sup> orbital on the central carbon holding a lone pair
A σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbital of one methyl group
An sp<sup>2</sup> orbital on the central carbon in the plane of the methyl groups
h: The cationic carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> with three σ bonds. Which of its orbitals is left over and how many electrons does it hold?
w: The cationic carbon uses three sp2 orbitals for its three C–C σ bonds and has one unhybridized 2p orbital that is empty. This low-energy empty orbital is the LUMO, and nucleophiles attack it from either face of the planar cation (which is why SN1 at a stereocenter gives racemization).
x: A carbocation has no lone pair, and its carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp<sup>3</sup>.
σ*<sub>C–H</sub> orbitals are much higher in energy than the empty p orbital; neighboring C–H bonds donate into the p orbital (hyperconjugation), not the reverse.
All three sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals are already used in C–C σ bonds; the only empty orbital is the p orbital perpendicular to that plane.

q: Which tagged carbon of chloroacetone carries the largest partial positive charge?
h: Count bonds to electronegative atoms, and remember that a C=O π bond is also polarized toward oxygen (C<sup>+</sup>–O<sup>−</sup> contributor).
w: The carbonyl carbon a is bonded to oxygen by both a σ and a π bond, and the resonance contributor C+–O− places a full + on it. Its partial positive charge is the largest, which is why nucleophiles add to C=O carbons. Carbon b is δ+ from one C–Cl bond, and the CH3 carbon c is only slightly affected. Answer: a.
x: The C–Cl bond makes b δ+, but one polar σ bond to Cl withdraws less than a σ + π bond to oxygen with a C+–O− contributor.
The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has no bond to an electronegative atom; it is only weakly δ+ by induction through the carbonyl carbon.
Carbon b has a polar C–Cl bond and c does not, so they cannot be equal; neither matches the carbonyl carbon.

q:
Consider the carbon–halogen bonds in CH3F, CH3Cl, CH3Br and CH3I.
I. The C–F bond is the shortest and strongest.
II. The C–I bond is the most polar.
III. The C–Br bond is longer than the C–Cl bond.
Which statements are true?
h: Bond length follows the size of the halogen; bond polarity follows the electronegativity difference.
w: Down group 17 the halogen atoms grow larger, so bond length increases (C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I) and orbital overlap with carbon decreases, so bond strength decreases. That makes I and III true. Polarity follows electronegativity: F (4.0) gives the most polar bond, while I (2.7) is barely more electronegative than C (2.5), so the C–I bond is the least polar. Answer: I and III only.
x: II is false: iodine's electronegativity is close to carbon's, so C–I is the least polar C–X bond, not the most.
II is false, and I is true; C–F is both the shortest and the strongest C–X bond.
II is false: C–F is the most polar bond and C–I the least.

q: These C8H10 isomers have similar boiling points (136–144 °C). Which one has by far the highest melting point?
h: Boiling depends on attractions in the liquid; melting also depends on how well the molecules fit together in a crystal.
w: Melting point depends strongly on how efficiently molecules pack in the solid. p-Xylene is the most symmetrical isomer (a center of symmetry), so it packs tightly and melts at about 13 °C. o-Xylene (−25 °C), m-xylene (−48 °C) and ethylbenzene (−95 °C) are less symmetrical and pack poorly. The boiling points, which depend on liquid-phase forces, are all similar. This symmetry effect is used to purify p-xylene industrially by crystallization.
x: o-Xylene has the largest dipole and the highest boiling point, but its lower symmetry gives poorer packing; it melts near −25 °C.
m-Xylene is less symmetrical than the para isomer and melts at about −48 °C.
The flexible ethyl group packs worst of all; ethylbenzene melts near −95 °C.

q: These compounds have nearly the same molar mass (58–60 g/mol). Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: Two of these hydrogen-bond. Which bond, N–H or O–H, is more polar?
w: Butane (I) has only dispersion forces (bp −1 °C). Propan-1-amine (II) hydrogen-bonds through N–H (bp 48 °C). Propan-1-ol (III) hydrogen-bonds through O–H, which is more polar because O is more electronegative than N, so its H bonds are stronger (bp 97 °C). Order: I < II < III.
x: N–H bonds are less polar than O–H bonds, so the amine forms weaker H bonds and boils lower than the alcohol.
The amine hydrogen-bonds while butane does not, so the amine boils well above butane.
This is the reverse; butane, with dispersion forces only, boils lowest.

q: Rank the three carbon–carbon bonds of (E)-hex-3-en-1-yne from shortest to longest: I = a–b, II = c–d, III = d–e.
h: Bond order matters most. For single bonds, compare the hybridization (s character) of the two carbons.
w: III is the C≡C triple bond (about 1.20 Å), the shortest. II is a single bond, but it joins an sp2 carbon to an sp carbon; the high s character of both orbitals pulls the nuclei together (about 1.43 Å). I is an ordinary sp3–sp3 single bond (about 1.53 Å). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is the reverse; higher bond order and higher s character both shorten a bond, so the triple bond is shortest.
The single bond II cannot be shorter than the triple bond III, even with sp<sup>2</sup>–sp hybridization.
The sp<sup>2</sup>–sp single bond (II) is shorter than the sp<sup>3</sup>–sp<sup>3</sup> single bond (I) because of its greater s character.
